# Scales

```{r}
#| include: false
source("R/setup.R")
```

What do you do when most of your values are close together at one end of an
axis, and a few are far away? You change the **scale**, which decides how a
number becomes a position. It is written inside the channel's parentheses,
beside the column, and not as an atom of its own:

```r
x(gdp, scale = "log")
```

A scale belongs to one channel, so it is written where that channel is bound.
There is no `scale()` atom to write separately. A separate atom would make you
name the channel twice, once to bind it and once to scale it. The two could then
name different channels by mistake: `gdp` bound to `x`, and the log scale written
for `y`.

Writing the scale on the binding also makes a sentence easier to read. To see
how `gdp` is placed, you look at `x(gdp, scale = "log")` and nowhere else.
Nothing else in the sentence can change it, and there is no second function to
look up.

## A scale is not a transform {#a-scale-is-not-a-transform}

A log scale is not the only way to spread out incomes that run from hundreds to
tens of thousands of dollars. You could take the logarithm of the column
yourself and plot the result. That is a different operation, and it changes
which numbers the ticks show.

`bin` and `mean` are **transforms**: they read your table and compute new
values from it. A scale produces no new values at all. It changes how far along
the axis a number lands and what the ticks say, and nothing else.

The difference is visible in the finished plot. The `gapminder_2007` table
holds one row for each of 142 countries in 2007, with its income per person
(`gdp`) and its life expectancy (`life`). Here is `gdp` plotted with a log
*scale*:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(gapminder_2007)
```

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  color(continent) +
  x_label("GDP per person") +
  title("Income and life expectancy: log scale")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, color by
continent."*

The axis reads 1K and 10K, that is, 1,000 and 10,000. Those are dollars, the
units you supplied.

The word *log* appears nowhere on the axis, and that is deliberate. The units
did not change, so the axis name does not say they did. The ticks are the only
sign: each is ten times the one before, so every step of the same length along
the axis multiplies the value by the same factor, here ten. Write
`x_label("GDP per person (log scale)")` when a reader needs the scale named in
words. The axis name is what you write with `x_label()`, and gog never writes
the scale into it.

Now the same picture, drawn from a column that already holds the logarithm.
The `gm_logged` table is `gapminder_2007` with one more column, `log_gdp`, the
base-10 logarithm of `gdp`:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(gm_logged)
```

```{r}
data(gm_logged) + point + x(log_gdp) + y(life) +
  color(continent) +
  title("The same shape, with the axis in log units")
```

*"Given the gm logged table: points, x is log gdp, y is life, color by
continent."*

Every point is in the same place as in the first plot, but the axis now reads
2.5 to 4.5. Those numbers are logarithms, not dollars. The tick at 3.0 is
where the first plot has 1K, because ten to the power of 3 is 1,000. The tick at
3.5 means ten to the power of 3.5. That is about 3,162 dollars, a number most
people need a calculator to find. On a log scale you need no calculation,
because the ticks are already in dollars.

So the choice depends on what the numbers stand for. Take the logarithm of the
column when that logarithm is itself the quantity of interest: a log-odds, a
decibel, a pH. Use a log scale when the numbers still count dollars or people,
and you only want to spread out values that run from hundreds to tens of
thousands.

## The order of a scale and a transform {#the-order-of-a-scale-and-a-transform}

Once a transform is in the plot, a scale is no longer only about display,
because gog must decide whether the transform computes on your numbers or on
their logarithms. gog follows one rule, and it has no per-transform exceptions:

> A transform groups by one axis and computes the values on the other. The scale is
> applied before the transform on the grouping axis, and after it on the
> measured axis.

For `bar * bin`, `x` is the grouping axis, because the rows are divided into bins
by their `x` values. `y` is the measured axis, where the counts go. So a log `x`
is applied before the bins are cut, and a log `y` after the counts are made.

### Scaling the grouping axis {#scaling-the-grouping-axis}

A histogram of income shows how that rule changes the result. Its bins have to
be cut somewhere, either in dollars or in the logarithms of those dollars.

`bin` groups by x, so a log x is applied first. The bins are cut on the
logarithms, not on the dollars. The upper end of each bin is then about 1.8
times its lower end. Every bar is therefore the same width,
and the bars fill the axis from end to end. The right plot below shows this.
The left plot is the same sentence on the default linear scale, so its bins
are cut in dollars:

```{r}
(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(gdp) +
   x_label("GDP per person") + title("Linear scale: bins cut in dollars")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(gdp, scale = "log") +
     x_label("GDP per person") + title("Log scale: bins cut on the logarithms"))
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by bin, x is gdp, beside the same with gdp
on a log scale."*

gog never draws the dollar bins on the left on a log axis. If it did, the first
bin, from 278 to about 5,700 dollars, which holds 69 of the 142 countries,
would cover more than half of the axis. The other eight bins would share the
narrow strip on the right, and the plot would look broken. That is why the
grouping axis is scaled first.

### The measured value keeps its own units {#the-measured-value-keeps-its-own-units}

Put the log on the measured axis instead and a different question follows. Does
a bar on a log scale stand for a sum of dollars, or for a sum of logarithms?

`sum` writes to y, so a log y is applied *after* the sum. The `receipts` table
holds four receipts from two stores: North's are 10 and 90, and South's are 1
and 9. So the two bars in this plot stand for 100 and 10:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(receipts)
```

```{r}
data(receipts) + bar * sum + x(store) + y(sales, scale = "log") +
  title("A sum is still a sum")
```

*"Given the receipts: bars derived by sum, x is store, y is sales on a log
scale."*

If the scale had been applied first, gog would have added the *logarithms*, and
a sum of logarithms is the logarithm of a product. North's bar would then show
900, ten times ninety, which is not North's total of 100. gog adds the dollars first
and scales the total afterwards, so `sum` reports a sum of dollars.

If you have used ggplot2, note the order, because ggplot2 does the opposite.
Under `scale_y_log10()`, a `stat_summary(fun = mean)` averages the logarithms of
the values. The result is a geometric mean, the average computed on the
logarithms. gog computes the summary in your data's units and scales the result,
so the number the bar stands for is the number you would get by taking the sum
or the mean yourself.

### `smooth`: a curve on a log axis {#smooth-a-curve-on-a-log-axis}

The grouping axis raises the same question for `smooth`: is the curve fitted to
dollars, or to their logarithms? On incomes that run from a few hundred dollars
to nearly fifty thousand, the answer changes the shape of the curve.

`smooth` groups by x, so with a log x the curve is fitted against log income.
Life expectancy rises by about the same amount for each tenfold rise in income,
so the curve on the right is close to a straight line. The curve on the left is
fitted to the same rows on the default linear scale, and it bends sharply near
10K:

```{r}
(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
   style(color = "lightgray") +
   line * smooth + x(gdp) + y(life) +
   x_label("GDP per person") + title("A trend fitted against dollars")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
     style(color = "lightgray") +
     line * smooth + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
     x_label("GDP per person") + title("A trend fitted against log income"))
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, and also a line derived by
smooth, x is gdp, y is life, beside the same with gdp on a log scale."*

### `straight`: a line on a log axis {#straight-a-line-on-a-log-axis}

By the rule above, a scale is applied before the transform on the grouping
axis and after it on the measured axis. So `straight`'s two axes are treated
differently. With a log x, the least-squares line is fitted to log income, so
it is drawn as a straight line. With a log y, the line would be fitted to life
expectancy in years and then drawn on the log axis, where it would bend. gog
refuses that sentence, because `straight` must draw a straight line:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_2007) + x(gdp) + y(life, scale = "log") +
  point + line * straight
```

[The least-squares line](transforms.qmd#straight-the-least-squares-line) shows
the line on a log x, and this refusal again.

## What a log scale refuses {#what-a-log-scale-refuses}

Some columns cannot take a log scale, and they are not rare: a depth that goes
below zero, a balance that went negative, a count of zero.

A logarithm is undefined at zero and below, so rows with such values have no
position on the axis. gog says so rather than dropping them quietly. The
`depth_readings` table holds four readings of depth and temperature, and two of
them have a depth of 0 or less: 0 and -4.

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(depth_readings)
```

```{r}
#| error: true
data(depth_readings) + point + x(depth, scale = "log") + y(temp)
```

The message names how many rows are affected and the smallest value in the
column, because "some of your data cannot be drawn" is not enough to act on.

A categorical column has no logarithm either, and it already gets a categorical
axis without being asked:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(continent, scale = "log") + y(life)
```

## Choosing the base {#choosing-the-base}

Not every quantity is best read in powers of ten. Ten is the usual base for
money and for population. But a sound's frequency doubles with every octave,
and a quantity that grows or shrinks continuously is counted in factors of
*e*.

`scale = "log"` means base 10 unless you say otherwise:

```r
x(freq, scale = "log", base = 2)
```

The base is a *number*, not a name. There is no `"log2"` or `"ln"` scale. One
`base` argument already covers every base, so a separate name for each would
add words without adding meaning. The same objection rules out ggplot2's
`scale_x_log10` family.

### The base changes the labels, not the picture {#the-base-changes-the-labels-not-the-picture}

You might expect a new base to move the points. It does not: each point keeps
its place along the axis. The base-2 logarithm of any value is always about
3.32 times its base-10 logarithm. gog places every value by where it falls
between the axis's two ends, so that fixed multiplier cancels. The transforms are unaffected too:
bins of equal width in base 2 are equal width in base 10, so `bar * bin` cuts
at the same values whichever base you name.

What the base actually chooses is where the gridlines fall and how they read.
Here are six frequencies, each one an octave above the one before it, on base
10 and then base 2:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(octaves)
```

```{r}
data(octaves) + point + x(freq, scale = "log") + y(level) +
  x_label("Frequency (Hz)") + title("Base 10: gridlines at 100, 1K")
```

*"Given the octaves: points, x is freq on a log scale, y is level."*

```{r}
data(octaves) + point + x(freq, scale = "log", base = 2) + y(level) +
  x_label("Frequency (Hz)") + title("Base 2: gridlines on every octave")
```

*"Given the octaves: points, x is freq on a log scale in base 2, y is level."*

Each point is at the same place along its axis. The second plot puts a
gridline on each doubling,
which is what "an octave" means. So for pitch, bits, or doubling times, base 2
puts a tick at every doubling, the unit you are counting.

### Natural log {#natural-log}

The natural base is for a quantity that grows or shrinks continuously at a
constant rate. The amounts in the `decay` table shrink by
a factor of *e* every hour, so there is one
gridline between each reading and the next. A change by a factor of *e* is
called an **e-folding**.

R has no constant named *e*, so you write `base = exp(1)`. The other three
bindings have one: Python's `math.e`, Julia's `ℯ`, and JavaScript's `Math.E`.

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(decay)
```

```{r}
data(decay) + point + x(amount, scale = "log", base = exp(1)) + y(hours) +
  x_label("Amount remaining") +
  title("Gridlines at each e-folding: one step is a factor of e")
```

*"Given the decay table: points, x is amount on a log scale in base e, y is
hours."*

Notice the labels: 1, then *e*, *e*^2^, *e*^3^, *e*^4^, not 2.718, 7.389, 20.086,
54.598.
That follows from one rule gog applies to every base:

> Write the value itself when it is a whole number with few digits; otherwise
> write the power.

Base 10 gives 1, 10, 100, 1K, 10K and so on, up to 100T. K means a thousand, M
a million, B a billion (10^9^) and T a trillion (10^12^). A number before a letter
has at most three digits, and no letter comes after T. So from 10^15^ upward, a
tick is labeled as a power instead, such as 10^15^. Base 2 gives 1, 2, 4 and so on, up
to 8388608. A number with more than seven digits is labeled as a power instead,
such as 2^24^. No power of *e* above 1 is a whole number, so every tick past
the first reads as a power, which is what a reader counting e-foldings wants. If
instead you want the axis to read 0, 1, 2, 3, the natural logarithms
themselves, you do not want a log scale at all. You want `log()`
applied to the column, and an axis labeled in log units, like the `log_gdp` plot in
[A scale is not a transform](#a-scale-is-not-a-transform). A scale keeps your
units; a column of logarithms changes them.

A base only means something as the base *of* a logarithm, so gog refuses one
that has no log scale to belong to:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(octaves) + point + x(freq, base = 2) + y(level)
```

## Time: a date column gets a calendar axis {#time-a-date-column-gets-a-calendar-axis}

A column of dates raises a question the other columns do not. Where do the
ticks go, and what do they say, when the units are years and months rather than
tens and hundreds?

The time scale is one you never have to write. A column of dates or date-times
*is* temporal, because its type already says so: a `Date` or a `POSIXct` in R,
a `date`, `datetime` or `datetime64` in Python, a `Date` or a `DateTime` in
Julia, and a `Date` in JavaScript. gog reads the calendar from the type, the
same way a column of text already gets a categorical axis. The `revenue` table
holds one year's sales for each of 26 years, 1994 to 2019, each dated June 30:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(revenue)
```

```{r}
data(revenue) + line + x(day) + y(sales) +
  title("Twenty-six years, ticked in years")
```

*"Given the revenue table: a line, x is day, y is sales."*

The sentence names no scale at all. Writing `scale = "time"` is allowed and adds
nothing, exactly like writing `scale = "linear"` on a number.

The ticks land on **calendar boundaries**, because the calendar does not count
in tens: a year has twelve months, and a week has seven days. An axis of years
steps 1, 2 or 5 like any number line. For units smaller than a
year those steps mean nothing: nobody reads an axis cut into fifths of a year.
Months step by 1, 2, 3 or 6, and each of those divides twelve. A gridline
therefore always falls on January, and a 3-month step marks each quarter. Days
step by 1 or 2. Weeks step by 1 or 2, and a week tick is always on a Monday. Hours step by 1, 3, 6
or 12, and each of those divides twenty-four, so a gridline always falls on
midnight. Minutes and seconds step by 1, 5, 15 or 30. The `six_weeks` table
holds 42 days of orders, starting on Friday, March 1, 2024:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(six_weeks)
```

```{r}
# six_weeks: daily orders for six weeks
data(six_weeks) + line + x(day) + y(orders) +
  title("Six weeks, ticked on Mondays")
```

*"Given the six weeks table: a line, x is day, y is orders."*

A tick is written in the unit of its step: `2010` for a year step, `Jan 2024`
for a month step, `Mar 4` for a day step. A column of dates never gets clock
ticks, however narrow its range. A column of date-times can, because it stores
a time of day. That is a `POSIXct` in R, a `datetime` in Python, a `DateTime` in
Julia, and in JavaScript a `Date` column whose values are not all midnight. The
`monitoring` table holds a load reading every hour for a day and a half:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(monitoring)
```

```{r}
data(monitoring) + line + x(at) + y(load) +
  title("A day and a half, ticked by the clock")
```

*"Given the monitoring table: a line, x is at, y is load."*

`00:00` happens every day, so that label names no particular day. The midnight
tick shows the date instead. Every other label on a time axis follows one rule:
*a tick is written in the unit of its step, and it leaves out what it shares
with its neighbors.*

### Bars on a date axis {#bars-on-a-date-axis}

Daily orders make a natural bar chart, one bar per day, and forty-two bars
raise the question of where the ticks go.

Bars positioned at dates are an ordinary time series. The ticks still come from
the calendar, and there is not a tick for every bar. Wilkinson's stock-price
example puts its ticks on Sundays rather than on every trading day
[@wilkinson2005], and gog ticks these six weeks at the start of each week:

```{r}
data(six_weeks) + bar + x(day) + y(orders) +
  title("Daily bars, weekly ticks")
```

*"Given the six weeks table: bars, x is day, y is orders."*

A bar never measures a date. A bar's *length* is an amount, and a moment in time
is not an amount. A bar "reaching" 2007 would be measured from 1970, the year a
stored date counts from, which nobody chose as a baseline. So the bars are
always placed along the dates, on whichever axis you write them. Write the dates
on `y` and the orders on `x`, and the same bars are horizontal:

```{r}
data(six_weeks) + bar + y(day) + x(orders) +
  title("Daily bars, drawn horizontally")
```

*"Given the six weeks table: bars, y is day, x is orders."*

With dates on one axis and a category on the other, a bar has nothing to
measure. Neither column is an amount. gog refuses it, and the message asks for a
continuous column in place of the category:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(six_weeks) + bar + x(day) + y(weekday)
```

### Marks on a date axis {#marks-on-a-date-axis}

A date is a moment, and most marks have no width along a date axis. A `point`,
a `line`, a `step`, an `area`, a `text` label and a `rule` are drawn at their
dates. An `interval` or a `ribbon` runs between two values on the other axis,
at each date.

Three marks have a width: `bar`, `box` and `zone`. On a date axis, each one
takes a slot as wide as the smallest distance between two dates in its table.
In a table with one row a day, the slot is one day. `style(gap = )` leaves a
share of the slot empty, as it does on a categorical axis. A date with no row,
such as a weekend in a table of trading days, stays empty, because a calendar
axis has a place for every date.

To give every date an equal slot, with no empty days, convert the dates to text
before the plot. A column of text gets a categorical axis, with one slot for
each value, in the order the values first appear in the table. The
[candlestick](marks/zone.qmd#the-candlestick) in the Zone chapter is drawn both
ways: one slot for each session, and on a calendar axis.

### What a time axis refuses {#what-a-time-axis-refuses}

A date is stored as a number underneath. You might therefore expect a date to
take a log scale, and a number to take a time scale. Neither is allowed.

A moment has no logarithm. The zero a stored date counts from is a convention: dates could be
counted from 1900 as easily as from 1970, and the same day would then have a
different logarithm. A number that changes with that choice measures nothing
about the day:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(revenue) + line + x(day, scale = "log") + y(sales)
```

gog can read the calendar off a date column, but `scale = "time"` cannot turn a
column that is not a date column into one. The engine cannot know whether a
number like the 52 in `sales` counts days, seconds or years since some
starting date:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(revenue) + point + x(sales, scale = "time") + y(sales)
```

Only the data says what the number counts, so the fix belongs in the data. Store the column as
dates or date-times, in your language's date or timestamp type. In R that is
`as.Date()` or `as.POSIXct()`. The chapters for
[Python](bindings/python.qmd#the-table), [Julia](bindings/julia.qmd#the-table)
and [JavaScript](bindings/javascript.qmd#the-table-and-its-name) name the types
in each.

For the same reason, a plain number cannot set the width of a bin on a time
axis. `bin(width = 7)` does not say whether 7 counts days or seconds. The engine
measures time in seconds, so these bins would be seven seconds wide, far too
thin to see:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(six_weeks) + bar * bin(width = 7) + x(day)
```

To cut a time axis into bins, give the number of bins instead: `bin(6)` cuts
these six weeks into six bins.

Time zones are never converted. The engine draws the clock time you gave it. In
R, a `POSIXct` is formatted in its own time zone when it is drawn, so the axis
shows the times your session showed you. In Python, a `datetime` is drawn at
the clock time it holds, and one with a time zone is drawn in its own zone. In
Julia, a `DateTime` holds no time zone, so it is drawn as written. In
JavaScript, a `Date` is drawn as your computer's clock shows it, in local time.
If two series must share an axis, put them in one time zone before plotting;
that decision belongs to the analysis, not the engine.

### Time on the other channels {#time-on-the-other-channels}

A scale answers *how far along?* on every channel that measures, and a date
column is no exception. Coloring rows by how recent they are is common. An axis
tick can read `Mar 4`, because the ticks beside it place it in a sequence. A
legend row is read on its own, so each row carries the full date:

```{r}
data(six_weeks) + point + x(day) + y(orders) + color(day) +
  title("Recent days, darker")
```

*"Given the six weeks table: points, x is day, y is orders, color by day."*

## The scales {#the-scales}

The chapter has used `linear`, `log` and `time` so far, and `category` comes
later, in [The column's type picks the axis](#the-columns-type-picks-the-axis).
The table names all four and what each one does.

| Scale | What it does |
|---|---|
| `linear` | Equal steps for equal differences. The default |
| `log` | Equal steps for equal ratios, on `x`, `y`, `color`, `size` and `opacity`, with any `base` above 1 |
| `time` | Positions dates and times, chosen from the column type: columns of dates and date-times, on every channel that measures |
| `category` | One slot per distinct value, chosen from the column type: columns of text, and columns with a declared order |

## The axis fits your data {#the-axis-fits-your-data}

Where should an axis end, on the data or on the next round number past it?
Padding to a round number leaves part of the panel blank, and implies that the
data reaches further than it does.

An axis shows round numbers on its ticks, but the *range* follows your data, not
the round numbers. Each tick is a round number that falls *inside* the data, or
at most a little past it into the margin. The axis does not extend to the next
multiple of ten only to end on a round number. A span of 1952–2007 is drawn as
1952–2007, with ticks at 1960, 1980 and 2000, not padded to 1940–2020 with a
third of the panel left blank. The `gapminder_asia` table holds five Asian
countries, each from 1952 to 2007. The plot draws the five as overlapping areas
of one color, because only the year axis matters here.
[Area](marks/area.qmd#multiple-series) tells the countries apart with color.

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(gapminder_asia)
```

```{r}
data(gapminder_asia) + area + x(year) + y(life) +
  group(country) + style(opacity = 0.4) +
  title("The year axis fits 1952–2007; the ticks fall inside it")
```

*"Given gapminder Asia: areas, x is year, y is life, grouped by country."*

Two more rules refine that fit. An end you do not state is set by the data's
smallest or largest value, and that end is a **free end**. A free end leaves a small margin, so a glyph never touches the panel
edge. A point at the exact maximum would otherwise be cut in half by that edge.
The plot uses the `gapminder_2007` table, shown in
[A scale is not a transform](#a-scale-is-not-a-transform):

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) + color(continent) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + title("No point touches the panel edge")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, color by continent."*

A baseline gets no margin. The area plot titled *The year axis fits
1952–2007* shows it: the shape starts on the panel's bottom edge, not a little
way above it. When a bar or an area measures from zero, the zero is part of
what it measures. A gap beneath it would show a stretch of axis below zero that
no bar can reach, so the baseline is on the panel edge.

An `area` also runs from the left edge of the panel to the right. The margin
exists so that a point at the end of an axis is not cut by the panel edge. An
area has no point to cut, and a margin beside it would show as an empty band,
so the area is drawn up to the edges. That is why the area plot spans the full
width while the scatterplot of incomes keeps its margins. A line keeps the
margin too, like a point, and so does an area drawn in the same plot as
points.

A label reaches past its value too, by the width of its letters. When a label
near a free end would not fit inside the panel, the axis is widened just enough to
hold its letters. Oceania has the longest bar below, and its label is printed
past the end of that bar. The labels are a `text` layer
([Number labels](marks/text.qmd#number-labels-the-value-on-each-mark)):

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + y(continent) + x(life) +
  text * mean + label(life, decimals = 1) + style(nudge = "right") +
  title("The life axis is widened to fit Oceania's label")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by mean, y is continent, x is life, and also
text derived by mean, label by life with 1 decimal place, with nudge right."*

Oceania's 80.7 ends just inside the panel's right edge. Only a free end is
widened. A baseline stays where it is. An end you state with
[`limits`](#limits-stating-the-range-yourself) also stays, and a label past it is
cut at the panel edge. A label whose letters take more than a quarter of the
panel is not given room either, and is cut.

## A scale is not only for axes {#a-scale-is-not-only-for-axes}

Most of this chapter has put a scale on an axis. But on a linear color ramp
most values can get nearly the same color, just as on a linear axis most points
can fall at one end. `x` and `y` turn a number into a position, but so do
`color`, `size` and `opacity`: a place on the ramp, a radius, an opacity. All
five answer *how far along?*, so all five take a scale. In three dimensions `z`
takes a scale too, but the engine does not draw a log `z`; see
[Space](space.qmd).

This matters most for a column spread across orders of magnitude. `population`
runs from about 200 thousand to 1.3 billion. On a linear ramp the median
country is in the bottom one percent of that range, so nearly every point
gets the same color:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  color(population) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + title("Linear color: nearly one flat color")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, color by
population."*

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  color(population, scale = "log") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + title("Log color: the whole ramp is used")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, color by
population on a log scale."*

Look again at the middle number in the color legends of the two plots titled
*Linear color* and *Log color*. On a linear ramp it is halfway between the two
ends. On a log ramp it is the *geometric* midpoint, √(min · max), the square
root of the smallest value times the largest: about 16M rather than 660M. The
label has to be the geometric midpoint, because it names the color drawn at the
middle of the ramp.

The same is true of `size`. With a linear scale, almost every point is drawn at
the smallest radius, and only China and India are large:

```{r}
(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
   size(population) + style(color = "steelblue") +
   x_label("GDP per person") + title("Linear size")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
     size(population, scale = "log") + style(color = "steelblue") +
     x_label("GDP per person") + title("Log size"))
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, size by
population, beside the same with population on a log scale."*

`shape`, `pattern` and `group` answer *which one?*, not *how far along?*: there
is no distance between a circle and a square. So gog refuses `scale` on all
three, as shown here for `shape`:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  shape(continent, scale = "log")
```

## `limits`: stating the range yourself {#limits-stating-the-range-yourself}

Every rule so far takes the range from the data. That is the right default, but
sometimes an axis should cover values that no row reaches. The `tide` table
holds a gauge's readings, one height every three hours from hour 1 to hour 22, so none falls at midnight. `polar()` draws an axis
as a circle, and [Polar](polar.qmd) teaches that space in full. Nothing in a
column of hours tells that circle that hour 24 is the same place as hour 0.
`limits` states the range the axis covers. The left plot below has no `limits`, and the right
plot states them:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(tide)
```

```{r}
((data(tide) + line + x(hour) + y(height) + polar() +
    title("Without limits: hours 1 to 22")) |
   (data(tide) + line + x(hour, limits = c(0, 24)) + y(height) + polar() +
      title("With limits: the whole day"))) +
  theme(width = 800, height = 420)
```

*"Given the tide: a line, x is hour, y is height, in polar, beside a line, x is
hour from 0 to 24, y is height, in polar."*

Without `limits`, one turn covers only 1 to 22, so the first and last readings
are drawn on the same spoke, at the top of the left circle. With `limits`, each
hour is drawn at its own fraction of the turn: hour 0 at the top, hour 6 a
quarter of the way around, hour 12 halfway. The curve
still does not close, and should not. The gauge took no reading at midnight, and
`limits` says what range the axis covers rather than inventing an observation.
The gap is in the readings, and the plot shows it at its true size, the three
hours from 22 to 1. [Polar](polar.qmd) describes three cases: two in which the
curve closes, and this one, in which it does not.

`limits` is written on the binding, beside `scale` and `base`, for the same
reason they are: the range belongs to one channel, and an atom of its own would
name that channel twice. A stated end is drawn exactly where you state it. The
margin exists to keep a glyph off the panel edge, and an end you chose is not a
data extreme that needs the room.

`limits` can widen the axis as easily as it narrows it. Nothing was dropped in
the plot titled "With limits: the whole day": the readings run 1 through 22 and all of them lie inside 0 through
24. Narrowing is the direction that removes rows, and gog reports how many rows
it removes:

```{r}
#| message: true
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, limits = c(0, 30000)) + y(life) +
  color(continent) + x_label("GDP per person") +
  title("Limits of 0 to $30,000")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp from 0 to 30000, y is life, color by
continent."*

The message above the plot is that report: it names how many rows fell outside
and what the limits were. The plot still draws, because removing those rows is
what you asked for, but gog does not remove data without saying so. Ask for
limits no row can satisfy and gog refuses instead, because the alternative is an
empty panel with axes drawn over nothing. No country has an income between one
and two million dollars:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, limits = c(1e6, 2e6)) + y(life)
```

Keeping every country in the plot and marking one group of them is a different
operation, and it has a different word. `limits` removes rows before the plot is
drawn. `brush` removes nothing: it dims the rows outside its range.
[Selection](selection.qmd) shows the two side by side.

When a transform computes the values on an axis, as `count` does, `limits`
leaves out each bar or point whose value falls outside the limits. `count` writes its
tally into a column named `count`, and you write `y(count)` to give that axis
its limits ([The name on a measure
axis](transforms.qmd#the-name-on-a-measure-axis)). Here the count axis stops at 40,
below Africa's count of 52:

```{r}
#| message: true
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(continent) + y(count, limits = c(0, 40))
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by count, x is continent, y is count from 0
to 40."*

Africa keeps its label and has no bar. A bar stopped at the top edge would show
40, not 52. The message above the plot says how many values were left out, so
the empty space above Africa does not mean zero.

You can state one end alone. Write `NA` for the end you leave out. `NA` is R's
word for a missing value; Python writes `None`, Julia `missing` and JavaScript
`null`, as the chapters for
[Python](bindings/python.qmd#how-values-are-written),
[Julia](bindings/julia.qmd#how-values-are-written) and
[JavaScript](bindings/javascript.qmd#how-values-are-written) show. The end you
leave out stays a free end, which is how you start an axis at zero and let the
top follow the data:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + point * mean + x(continent) + y(life, limits = c(0, NA)) +
  title("y from zero, top still fitted to the data")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: points derived by mean, x is continent, y is life from
0."*

`limits` reaches more than the axes. The range is a property of the scale, so
`limits` reaches every channel that measures. That is how you keep one color ramp the
same across plots built from different data. Here the legend runs from 100K to
2B, wider than the data, which runs from about 200 thousand to 1.3 billion:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  color(population, scale = "log", limits = c(1e5, 2e9)) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + title("A ramp fixed from 100K to 2B")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, color by
population on a log scale from 1e5 to 2e9."*

On a categorical axis `limits` is refused, and the refusal names the two ways to
get what you meant. A category has no range to lie inside. Choosing *which*
categories appear is filtering your table, and choosing what order they appear
in is `order()`.

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(continent, limits = c(0, 3)) + y(life)
```

## The column's type picks the axis {#the-columns-type-picks-the-axis}

The time section showed that a column of dates gets a calendar axis without
being asked. A column of text gets its own axis in the same way, and this
section states the rule behind both. Other tools, ggplot2 among them, make you
name a scale whenever you want to change one, so you may expect to write
`scale = "category"`.

The four scales are not all chosen the same way. You ask for `log`. A continuous
column gets `linear` when you ask for nothing. You do not ask for `time` or `category`:
gog reads those off the column. A column of dates gets a calendar axis, and a
column of text gets one slot per distinct value.

You may still write them. As with `scale = "time"` on a date column, writing
`scale = "category"` on a categorical column is allowed and changes nothing.
The plot below is identical to the same sentence with the scale left off:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(continent, scale = "category") + y(life) +
  title("Writing it changes nothing")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by mean, x is continent as a category, y
is life."*

What you cannot do is use a scale to contradict the column. Ask for a
categorical axis on a continuous column and gog refuses:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "category") + y(life)
```

The reason behind that refusal also explains the others in this chapter. A
scale says *how* a measured column is placed. The column's type decides whether
the axis measures at all. So `log` on a categorical column is refused, and
`time` on a column that is not a date column is refused. A date column cannot
be turned back into raw numbers by asking for `linear` either:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(revenue) + line + x(day, scale = "linear") + y(sales)
```

None of those refusals offers another scale. Each tells you to change the
column or remove the scale, because the column's type is what the axis reads.

There are two things you might mean by "draw this number as categories", and
there is a different answer for each. For one slot per distinct value, declare
the column's categories: a factor in R, a pandas `Categorical` in Python, a
`CategoricalArray` in Julia, and `ordered()` in JavaScript, all shown in
[Data](data.qmd#declaring-the-order-of-categories). For intervals of numbers, use `bin`,
which cuts the column into intervals and is covered in
[Transforms](transforms.qmd).

## `tick_count`: how many ticks the axis aims for {#tick_count-how-many-ticks-the-axis-aims-for}

An axis picks about five ticks by default, and you can also choose how many
ticks it gets. A crowded axis is easier to read with fewer; an axis someone will
take numbers from is easier with more. How many ticks an axis gets is a
property of the scale. So `tick_count` is written on the binding, beside
`scale`, `base` and `limits`, and not in `theme()`, which sets how the whole plot looks.

```{r}
(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, tick_count = 3) + y(life) +
   x_label("GDP per person") + title("A low count: the shape, not the numbers")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, tick_count = 12) + y(life) +
     x_label("GDP per person") + title("A high count: for reading values off"))
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp with 3 ticks, y is life, beside the
same with 12 ticks."*

The count is a target, not an exact number. The count sets the *step* between
ticks, and the step is then rounded to 1, 2 or 5 times a power of ten. So asking
for eight ticks on an axis from 0 to 100 gives a step of 10, and eleven ticks.
Still, a higher count never gives fewer ticks than a lower one. Every tick is a round number. The count also has an upper
limit: an axis draws at most 26 ticks. If the rounded step would give more than
26 ticks, the engine uses a larger round step. The axis is still labeled from
one end to the other, and a message names both steps.

Both plots above cover the same range. That is the rule the count obeys: it
changes how densely an axis is *labeled*, never where the axis stops. Ask for
two ticks and the axis does not shrink to the two values it draws. The plot
below reads the `gapminder_asia` table, shown in [The axis fits your
data](#the-axis-fits-your-data):

```{r}
data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(year, tick_count = 2) + y(life) +
  group(country) + style(opacity = 0.4) +
  title("Two ticks, and still 1952 to 2007")
```

*"Given gapminder Asia: lines, x is year with 2 ticks, y is life, grouped by
country."*

A log axis and a date axis take a count too, but their steps are rounded to
different values. On a log axis the ticks can be at every power of the base, or
skip one or more powers between them. In base 10 they can also be at 1, 2 and 5
times each power. A date axis uses calendar steps, such as a day, a week, a
month or a year. [The time section](#time-a-date-column-gets-a-calendar-axis)
describes these steps. On these two axes, the engine picks the step whose number
of ticks is closest to your count.

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log", tick_count = 12) + y(life) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + title("Seven ticks: 1, 2 and 5 times each power")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale with 12 ticks, y is
life."*

The sentence asks for twelve ticks, and the axis draws seven. In base 10 no log
step is finer than 1, 2 and 5 times each power, so seven is the closest count to
twelve. Without a count, this axis reads only 1K and 10K, as at the start of the
chapter.

A date axis takes a count too. The plot uses the `six_weeks` table, shown in
[the time section](#time-a-date-column-gets-a-calendar-axis):

```{r}
data(six_weeks) + line + x(day, tick_count = 3) + y(orders) +
  title("Three ticks: one every two weeks")
```

*"Given the six weeks table: a line, x is day with 3 ticks, y is orders."*

By default these six weeks get a tick every Monday, six in all. Asked for three,
the axis steps two weeks at a time, still on Mondays.

A categorical axis has one tick per category, so the data sets the count and
you do not. The refusal names the same two fixes the `limits` refusal named:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(continent, tick_count = 3) + y(life)
```

A legend is not an axis, and it takes no tick count. `limits` reaches every
channel that measures, because every one of them has a range of values; `tick_count`
reaches only the three position channels that draw an axis: `x`, `y` and `z`. A
color legend writes three numbers, both ends and the middle, and the scale,
linear or log, sets their values, not a count you choose. The middle number is
the midpoint explained in [A scale is not only for
axes](#a-scale-is-not-only-for-axes): the label for the color drawn halfway along the
ramp. So gog refuses a tick count on `color()`, `size()` or `opacity()`: they
draw no axis, so there are no ticks to count.

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  color(population, tick_count = 3)
```

### Crowding in the plane and in the cube {#crowding-in-the-plane-and-in-the-cube}

A flat panel and a cube follow one rule for crowded numbers: no number may be
printed over another. A flat continuous axis draws every tick it chose, as long
as no two numbers overlap. Where panels are side by side, a number at the end of
an axis that would reach past its panel is moved toward the middle of its own
panel. In narrow panels, such as the five panels of a plot
faceted by continent ([Faceting](faceting.qmd)), the numbers can still overlap.

The axis then draws fewer numbers, and the ticks and gridlines of the others are
left out too. The numbers it keeps are the ones a larger round step would
choose, so 0, 10K, 20K, 30K and 40K become 0, 20K and 40K. A number left out can
be read from the numbers on either side, so no message is printed. If you stated
a `tick_count`, a message says how many ticks were drawn. A map's axes follow
the same rule. A polar plot, and an axis freed with `free = TRUE`, still draw
every number they chose.

The sentence below asks for twelve ticks, but each panel has room for three,
and a message says so:

```{r}
#| message: true
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, tick_count = 12) + y(life) |
  facet(continent)
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp with 12 ticks, y is life, split into
panel columns by continent."*

A cube can also have too little room for its numbers. In a 3-D plot
([Space](space.qmd)), each axis is longer or shorter depending on the viewing
angle. Turning the cube lengthens one axis and shortens another. The cube then
draws as many numbers as fit and leaves the rest out. When a count you stated
cannot fit, the engine says so rather than quietly drawing fewer.

Names on a categorical axis follow the same rule: no name may be printed over
another. The axis tries to name every category, and a name is usually much wider
than a number. When names do not fit side by side, a flat axis first turns them
90 degrees, to read upward. A turned name needs room along the axis only for its
height, not its width. When even turned names are too close, the flat axis
leaves some out, as the cube does. It draws one name in every two or three, each
with its tick, and prints a message. The 142 countries of 2007 do not fit, even
turned:

```{r}
#| message: true
data(gapminder_2007) + bar + x(country) + y(life)
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: bars, x is country, y is life."*

Every bar is still drawn, and a bar without a name keeps its place between two
named ones. The message gives two ways to name every country: put `country` on
the y axis in a taller plot, or draw fewer rows.

## `percent`, `short` and `decimals`: writing the numbers {#percent-short-and-decimals-writing-the-numbers}

An axis chooses how to write its own numbers, and so does a legend. Most of the
time their choice is easy to read. When it is not, three arguments on the
binding choose how the numbers are written, beside `scale`, `limits` and
`tick_count`. `percent = TRUE` writes a number as a percent. `short = TRUE`
writes a large number with K for thousands, M for millions, B for billions and T
for trillions. `decimals` sets how many decimal places each number has. A
binding without any of the three keeps the axis's own choice.

A share is the clearest case. `proportion` gives each bar its share of all the
rows, a number between 0 and 1, and the axis writes 0.0 to 0.3. As a percent,
the same axis writes 0% to 30%. The transform writes the `y`
column and names it `proportion`, so the argument goes on `y(proportion)`:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * proportion + x(continent) +
  y(proportion, percent = TRUE) + title("Each continent's share of the countries")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by proportion, x is continent, y is
proportion written as a percent."*

Only the numbers on the axis change. Each bar is as tall as it would be without
`percent`, and `limits` stays in the column's own units: `limits = c(0, 0.5)`
means 0 to 0.5, which the axis writes as 0% to 50%.

`short` matters on an axis whose numbers are large and close together. The
`two_readings` table holds France's rows for 2002 and 2007:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(two_readings)
```

The ticks are half a million apart, and the axis chooses one letter for all of
them from that distance. Half a million is less than a million, so the letter
is K: 60000K, 60500K and 61000K. With `short = TRUE`, each tick's letter comes
from the tick's own size, so the same ticks are 60M, 60.5M and 61M:

```{r}
data(two_readings) + line + point + x(year) + y(population, short = TRUE) +
  title("France: about 60 million people")
```

*"Given the two readings: a line and also points, x is year, y is population
written short."*

All three arguments work on a legend as well as on an axis. The color legend of
`gdp` writes 49.4K, 24.8K and 277.6 by default. With `decimals = 0` it writes
49K, 25K and 278:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(continent) + y(life) + color(gdp, decimals = 0)
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: points, x is continent, y is life, color by gdp with 0
decimal places."*

On an axis, `decimals` keeps the letter the axis chose and changes only the
number of decimal places. A population axis that writes 500M and 1000M writes
500.0M and 1000.0M with `decimals = 1`. If the places you ask for cannot tell
two ticks apart, the axis draws fewer ticks. With `decimals = 0`, ticks at 0,
0.5 and 1 would write 0, 0 and 1, so the axis keeps only the whole numbers.
When that would leave fewer than two ticks, gog refuses the plot and names the
axis's range, because one tick shows a place but no direction. The share axis
above runs from 0 to 0.385, past its last tick at 0.3, so 0 is its only whole
number:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * proportion + x(continent) +
  y(proportion, decimals = 0)
```

`percent` and `short` are two ways to write one number, so gog refuses the pair:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * proportion + x(continent) +
  y(proportion, percent = TRUE, short = TRUE)
```

The three arguments work only where an axis or a legend writes plain numbers. A
date axis writes dates, so there is no number to write another way, and gog
refuses the three arguments there. A log axis writes the powers of its base or the
values they name, and a map writes degrees. gog does not yet write those in another way, so it refuses
the three arguments there too, and the message says so. `label()`, which sets the text
a `text` mark prints, takes the same three arguments, as
[the text chapter](marks/text.qmd) shows.

On a web page, the three arguments also set how a number is written on the
card that shows a point's values, as [Pointing at a
mark](selection.qmd#pointing-at-a-mark) explains. With `x(gdp, short = TRUE)`,
the card writes Germany's gdp as 32.2K rather than 32170.37442. Without any of
the three, the card writes the number as it is in your table.

## `axis`: leaving an axis out {#axis-leaving-an-axis-out}

A person looking at a plot reads a position's value from an axis, as they read
a color's value from a legend. Sometimes they do not need the axis. On a map,
they find a place by
its shape and its neighbors, not by its longitude and latitude. Write
`axis = FALSE` on the binding, beside `scale` and `limits`, and the axis is left
out: its tick marks, its numbers and its name. The map below draws
`world_borders`, which holds one row for each point along a coastline or a
border:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(world_borders)
```

```{r}
data(world_borders) + path + x(lon, axis = FALSE) + y(lat, axis = FALSE) +
  group(piece) + map() + title("The coastlines, without axes")
```

*"Given the world borders: paths, x is lon without an axis, y is lat without an
axis, grouped by piece, in the map space."*

The scale is unchanged, so every point is drawn where it would be with the
axes. The panel takes the room the axes would have used. The gridlines stay, and
so does the frame: the two lines along the bottom and the left of the panel.
Both belong to the whole plot rather than to one axis.
[`theme()`](style.qmd#axes-legends-gridlines-and-the-frame) removes them with
`grid = "none"` and `frame = "none"`. In [Map](map.qmd#one-state-over-three-elections),
three small maps of Ohio leave out both axes, the gridlines and the frame.

`axis` is written on the three positions, `x`, `y` and `z`, because they are
the channels that draw an axis. On any other channel gog refuses it and names
the three. The name is part of the axis, so gog refuses `x_label()` for an axis
that is left out, even `x_label("")`:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, axis = FALSE) + y(life) +
  x_label("GDP per person")
```

## In short {#in-short}

A scale changes where a number is drawn, never the number itself. `limits`
states the range a channel covers, and narrowing it removes rows and reports how
many. `tick_count` is a target. A crowded axis draws fewer numbers, and a crowded
categorical axis turns its names first. `axis = FALSE` leaves an axis out and
keeps its scale. `percent`, `short` and `decimals` change only how the numbers
are written.

## What comes next {#what-comes-next}

A scale decides how far along a channel a number lands. It does not decide
which visual property shows the column.
[Channels](channels.qmd) covers that: which property carries a column, and what
guide it gets.
